chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu Basir said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who trimmed one of his fingernails while he was in the state of Ihram. He said: 'Upon him is, for every nail, the value of a Mudd of food, until they reach ten. If he trimmed the nails of both his hands entirely, then upon him is the blood of a sheep.' I said: 'If he trimmed the nails of both his feet and both his hands entirely?' He said: 'If he did that in one sitting, then upon him is one blood (offering). And if he did it separately in two sittings, then upon him are two bloods (offerings).'

key_terms.دَمُ شَاةٍ: The blood of a sheep (sacrifice of a sheep)
key_terms.قَلَّمَ: Trimmed or cut (specifically nails or hair)
key_terms.قِيمَةُ مُدٍّ: The value of a Mudd (a measure of volume/weight of food)
key_terms.مَجْلِسٍ: Sitting or session (a period of time spent in one place)
key_terms.مُحْرِمٌ: One in the state of Ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah)

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for trimming nails while in the state of Ihram during Hajj?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* outlines the specific fidya for trimming nails while in Ihram, distinguishing between minor infractions (a small food penalty per nail) and major ones (sacrificing a sheep for all hand or foot nails). It further clarifies that the liability for multiple sacrifices arises only if the full sets are trimmed in separate sessions, reflecting the juristic principle of distinguishing between continuous and discrete acts of violation. This detailed breakdown highlights the precision of Shia fiqh in calculating expiations based on both the extent of the act and its temporal continuity.
